title: Mówi się · znam go
note: C1 Block 3, unit 5 (C1-SPINE spine O6, B2-SPINE inbox item 19). ONE NEW STRING IN THE WHOLE UNIT: jego. RECOGNITION-LEANING AND SHAPE-BASED THROUGHOUT - the a2_jechac / b2_sie_impersonal treatment the spine names, two shapes shown as a picture and no rule claimed. The rejected alternative was a full clitic-position and topic-comment treatment, killed by the AGENTS line that killed the fleeting-e rule in b2_gen_pl_full: this learner gets no value from a rule he cannot trust. THE UNIFYING INSIGHT THE UNIT IS BUILT ON is that the short object pronouns and sie behave the SAME WAY - both lean on the word in front of them, both sit after the verb when nothing else opens the clause, both move in front of the verb when something does, and NEITHER CAN OPEN A CLAUSE. b2_sie_impersonal had already shown sie's two shapes as a table fact; this unit shows that go/ja/mu do it too, which turns two memorised habits into one picture. THE HARDEST DISCIPLINE IN THIS PACK IS NEGATIVE AND IT SHAPED KONTROLA: a word-order unit can very easily mark natural Polish WRONG. b2_pron_acc's own note records that it avoided short pronouns with noun subjects entirely because 'Mama kocha cie would be marked where Mama cie kocha is neutral, and choosing between them is a word-order fact, not a pronoun fact'. MARKED IS NOT UNGRAMMATICAL, so NO MERELY-MARKED STRING IS EVER OFFERED AS A WRONG ANSWER anywhere in the pack. Mama zna go. appears in no distractor. Every wrong choice is either genuinely illegal (a short form opening a clause - Go znam., Mu mama zna.), a real form in the wrong case (Znam ci., Mama go pomaga., Tata jej lubi.), or a different sentence with a different meaning (Tu nie pali. = he is not smoking here). The neutral order Mama go zna. is therefore TAUGHT ON A SLIDE AS A PICTURE and produced in Pisanie and Uzycie, but the learner is never asked to condemn its alternative. PAYS FOUR NAMED FENCES AT ONCE: b2_pron_acc's ('the fuller story is left where B2-SPINE's C1 list puts it, item 19'), a2_sie's NO CLITIC-PLACEMENT RULES, b2_sie_impersonal's refusal to claim sie goes second in the clause - which this pack also refuses, showing only the two attested shapes and no third - and the INVERTED COUNTED SUBJECT (W domu bylo piec okien) held by BOTH b2_num_subject and b2_plural_gym. The counted-subject slide adds no agreement fact: the neuter singular for 5-and-up and the ordinary plural for 2-4 are b2_num_subject's, recycled, and the only new thing is that the place phrase can stand in front. ADJECTIVES ARE ABSENT from every counted phrase for the same reason b2_num_subject gave - a genitive plural adjective is C1 Block 2 material and this unit sits before it on the path. jego is taught for ONE job only: it is the form that CAN open a clause, which is what makes the emphasis possible; the rest of the long-form paradigm is not opened, and jemu is verified NEW and stays out.

intro.title: The endings already say who did what — so the order says something else
intro.body:
In English the order of the words IS the grammar: "Dad helps Mum" and "Mum helps Dad" are different sentences because the words moved. Polish does not need word order for that job, because the endings have already done it.

So Polish spends its word order on something English handles with the voice: what is being emphasised, and what is old news. Moving a word to the front puts weight on it.

That freedom has one important limit, and it is what this unit is actually about. The SHORT words — go, ją, mu, się — cannot be moved anywhere you like. They lean on the word in front of them, and there are exactly two places they turn up.

rows: he is moved to the front, so the weight falls on him
Dad is the one Mum helps.
same endings, same meaning — different emphasis

intro.title: The short words lean backwards — so they never come first
intro.body:
go, ją, je, mu, mi, ci, cię are short and unstressed. They have to lean on something already said, which means there must be a word in front of them.

That gives exactly two shapes. If the verb opens the sentence, the pronoun follows it: Znam go. If a subject or another word opens the sentence, the pronoun leans on that instead and stands before the verb: Mama go zna.

What you cannot do is start with one. Go znam is not a Polish sentence — there is nothing for it to lean on.

rows: between the subject and the verb
between the subject and the verb
between the subject and the verb

intro.title: się does exactly the same thing
intro.title_pl: Nazywam się Anna. · Jak się nazywasz?
intro.body:
This is worth seeing side by side with the slide before, because it turns two separate habits into one picture.

się is short and unstressed too, and it behaves identically. Verb first, and się follows it: Nazywam się Anna. Something else first — a question word, a place word — and się leans on that instead, in front of the verb: Jak się nazywasz? Gdzie się kupuje bilet? Tu się nie pali.

You have been producing both shapes since A1 without being told they were a pattern. There is no third shape here to learn, and nothing to work out sentence by sentence.
intro.body_pl: Jak się masz? · Gdzie się kupuje bilet?

rows: Mówi się, że sklep jest zamknięty.

intro.title: To put the weight on him, you need the long form
intro.body:
Emphasis needs a word that can be stressed, and go cannot be. So Polish keeps a second, longer form for exactly this job, and it is the one that can stand at the front.

jego is the long form of go; ciebie is the long form of cię, which you already have. Both can open a sentence, and when they do, that is the emphasis.

The short form is the ordinary one and remains what you use nearly all the time. Reach for the long form only when you want the weight, the way English would say HIM rather than him.

rows: I know him. → HIM I know.
I know you. → YOU I know.

intro.title: A counted subject likes to come last
intro.body:
One more shape, and it is the one an English speaker is least likely to guess.

When you say how many of something there were somewhere, Polish usually puts the place first and the counted phrase last: W domu było pięć okien. English does the same trick with "there" — "there were five windows in the house" — so the shape is familiar even though the words are not.

The verb agreement is the one you already know and nothing here changes it: five and above takes the neuter singular było, two to four takes the ordinary plural były.

intro.title: What to carry away
intro.title_pl: Mama go zna. · Jak się nazywasz?
intro.body:
Three things, and none of them is a rule you have to apply word by word.

The endings carry who did what, so moving a word changes the emphasis and not the meaning. The short words — go, ją, je, mu, mi, ci, cię and się — lean backwards, so they sit after the verb when the verb comes first and in front of it when anything else does. And if you want to put the weight on a person, use the long form, because only the long form can stand at the front.

Where Polish leaves you a genuine choice, both orders are correct. This unit is about the places where there is no choice.
intro.body_pl: Znam go. · Mama go zna. · Jego znam.

rows: verb first → short word after it
something else first → short word before the verb
question word first → się before the verb
weight on the person → the long form, at the front
only the long form can be stressed
how many, somewhere → place first, count last

quiz.prompt: HIM I know — the weight on him →
quiz.explain: Only a long form can stand at the front, because only a long form can be stressed. go, mu and cię are short — they need a word in front of them to lean on.

quiz.prompt: YOU I know — the weight on you →
quiz.explain: ciebie is the long form of cię, and it is the one that can open the sentence. ci is the Dative and belongs to a different slot altogether.

quiz.prompt: I know him — the plain sentence, no emphasis →
quiz.explain: The verb opens the sentence, so the short pronoun leans on it and follows. znać acts on an object, so it takes the Accusative go — mu and ci are Dative forms.
Mama opens the sentence, so go leans on Mama and stands in front of the verb. Starting with go is the one thing that is not possible.
Same shape as Mama go zna. jej is the Dative and Genitive form; lubić acts on an object, so it needs the Accusative ją.
pomagać chooses the Dative, so the pronoun is mu, not go or jego. Its position is the ordinary one — after the subject, before the verb.
A plural subject changes nothing about where the short word stands.
The question word opens the clause, so się leans on it and stands in front of the verb. This is the order you have been producing since A1 in Jak się masz?
Nothing stands in front of the verb here, so się follows it. And się can no more open a sentence than go can.
Tu opens the clause, so się leans on it. Tu nie pali. is a different sentence — it means he is not smoking here.

quiz.prompt: There were five windows in the house. →
quiz.explain: Five and above takes the neuter singular było and the Genitive plural okien. Nothing about putting the place first changes that.

quiz.prompt: There were two windows in the house. →
quiz.explain: Two to four keeps the ordinary plural — były dwa okna — exactly as it did when the counted phrase stood at the front.
